newsitem.title: USA: Fed's Meyer says economic growth above trend rate.
newsitem.headline: Fed's Meyer says economic growth above trend rate.

text.p: U.S. economic expansion continued into the second quarter with solid momentum and now seems to be growing at an unsustainably strong rate, Federal Reserve Governor Laurence Meyer said on Thursday.

In a speech prepared for delivery to the Forecasters Club of New York, Meyer said first-quarter growth seems to have been least as strong as the fourth quarter's 3.8 percent annual rate and the momentum carried into the current second quarter.
"In short, the economy appears to be growing at an unsustainable above-trend rate," Meyer said.
A text of his remarks was released in Washington.

Meyer, who stressed he was speaking for himself, said he had supported a preemptive hike in short-term interest rates on March 25 by the policysetting Federal Open Market Committee out of concern about where capacity use rates and inflation were headed in the absence of a policy change.
He said that "persistent strength in aggregate demand" had persuaded him that a period of sustained above-trend growth had begun that might push utilization rates up and unemployment down.
He said the Fed must be prepared to pursue a monetary policy that "leans against the wind" to prolong the expansion.
"This requires that real interest rates rise as long as growth is above-trend and utilization rates are rising," he said.
The Fed considers growth in a range of 2 percent to 2-1/4 percent a year can be safely sustained without firing up inflation that could bring the expansion to an end.
Meyer said unemployment has "recently been inching lower" and may have dropped below NAIRU, the non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment.
"I suspect that the unemployment rate is now below NAIRU," Meyer said, adding it may have been below it for a while.

Meyer said that core inflation remains at a cyclical and a 30-year low, a performance he termed "extraordinary," but cautioned several factors that have restrained wages and prices so far may be less potent in future.

For example, the dollar's appreciation may make import prices decline further but its restraining impact on inflation may wane. Similarly, health care and benefit costs are "the least likely to continue" as a damper in inflation in view of recent surveys of health care insurance premiums, Meyer said.
He said the labor force has grown rapidly as participation rates rose but said that was unlikely to continue.

Some labor force growth likely resulted from efforts by state governments to get people off welfare, so that recent strength in output growth didn't result in a sharp rise in resource use rates, Meyer said.
Though labor force growth may wind down, "output growth must slow from recent levels to prevent further increases in utilization rates," Meyer said.

With wages rising, Meyer said the first-quarter Employment Cost Index, to be released by the Labor Department next Tuesday, bears special watching for signs of a bottoming out of the recent slowing in the pace of increase of benefit costs.

Meyer said the Fed doesn't expect higher long-term rates to carry the load of damping down demand. He also said that at times, the central bank considers the bond market misreads the economy's strength.

"While monetary policy cannot be a slave to the bond market, when the cyclical state of the economy suggests the desirability of a pro-cyclical response in interest rates, the Federal Reserve should pat the bond market on the back and appreciate its help, but not expect the bond market to carry the entire burden," Meyer said.
